subsubtopic: PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF HIGHWAY SERVICE DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has come to my attention that Canada Post plans to cancel its highway service deliveries to small communities in Ontario on Saturday and Sunday, effective October 1, next. This will mean that residents will have to wait until Monday, and in some cases Tuesday, for their mail. Many of these residents receive their unemployment and pension cheques on Saturdays. It is unfair for these people, who are already in a tight financial situation, to wait any longer than is necessary.
I believe that Canada Post will eventually close down its Saturday wicket service, using as logic: why stay open when there is no incoming and outgoing mail?
While 1 can understand that Canada Post is trying to eliminate its large deficit, I do not believe that residents in smaller communities should be made to suffer. Surely there must be other alternatives, besides reducing this vital service.
1 strongly oppose the proposed cancellation of highway service deliveries on weekends and 1 would encourage my colleagues in Parliament, and residents of Ontario, to take the necessary measures in order to ensure the reversal of this decision.

subsubtopic: LOSS OF TAXPAYER'S PAYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this Liberal Government confiscates money from a private bank account without notice to the owner, loses or steals $1,000, destroys the departmental records, and then glibly declares, "The case is closed"!
In 1975 a Canadian citizen, through the Mercantile Bank in Calgary, mailed a $1,000 cheque to Revenue Canada as an instalment payment. The cheque was stamped by Revenue Canada and credited to his account. Then someone in the Department decided that the cheque had been credited to the
wrong account, and so it was transferred. The citizen and his accountant notified the Department of the mistake, and continued to do so for several weeks, and were told that it was a simple computer mistake and would be corrected shortly.
It was corrected shortly all right, the Liberal way. Revenue Canada, without notice to or approval of the citizen, took $ 1,000 out of his account and credited it to his taxes.
During this dispute the records of Revenue Canada moved from Calgary to Winnipeg, and the citizen was told that the records had been destroyed and the case was closed.
The Minister of Revenue now parrots the statement and tells me that the case is closed. This is a complete cover-up by someone in Revenue Canada; no file should be destroyed when it is in dispute. The Government has a responsibility to replace this $1,000. Everyone knows this Liberal Government is money-hungry, but has it sunk so low as to condone the theft of $1,000 from an ordinary hard-working citizen, or to make him pay the same bill twice?
Honesty, honour, justice, are all I ask.

subsubtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM SPRAYING PROGRAM IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government will undoubtedly be aware of last week's Nova Scotia Supreme Court decision which basically gave the green light to both the provincial Government and the forest industry of Nova Scotia to recommence widespread spraying with 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T over populated areas in order to combat spruce budworm infested forest areas. This decision has obvious and serious forestry, environmental, and health implications, not only for Nova Scotia but also for the forest industry and related communities and regions across Canada. Yet the silence from the Government has been deafening.
Surely the Minister of Environment (Mr. Caccia), who is also responsible for forestry, has at least been able to consult with himself in his two separate roles, and hopefully he has also discussed this serious matter with his Cabinet Colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). If so, why have we not heard a word from him? Perhaps one of the reasons is the schizophrenic nature of his portfolio, which includes both forestry and environment.
1 hope that the obvious contradiction of having these two Departments under one Minister will cause the Government to reconsider the many submissions from the Canadian Institute of Forestry, the Canadian Forestry Association, the IWA, and

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RESTORATION OF PASSENGER SERVICES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a century ago Sir John A. Macdonald united this country by building a railroad from coast to coast. Two years ago the Grits began the process of dismantling that symbol of national unity when they announced a sharp reduction in passenger rail service.
The announcement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) that the Government is considering restoring service on two VIA Rail lines, one originating in his own constituency, is an indication that we are fast approaching an election. Canadians who were affected by the cuts will not forget the manner in which the disruptions were unilaterally imposed without parliamentary debate.
If the Minister is serious about demonstrating his good faith he will restore service to all lines that were cut, forgetting any silly review process. He will also open up the books of the public railway to the Auditor General, notwithstanding the recent remarks of Jack Horner.
Other countries are improving their rail service and conserving fuel, while this Government persists in promoting the most costly and energy wasteful forms of transportation. My constituents in Simcoe South know full well what it feels like to be deprived of a vital transportation service after losing the Barrie to Toronto run.
Canadians demand a restoration of an efficient national passenger rail service and they want it now, not when it suits the political ambitions of the Grit Party.

subsubtopic: SCENARIO OF PLAY GAME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last night members of all three political Parties took part in the playing of a new game called "Poleconomy"-the game of Canada. The results of this game were such that I feel a responsibility to inform all Members of the House and the people of Canada of its outcome.
The Conservative Party was represented by the former President of the Treasury Board and the previous Finance critic, the Liberals were represented by the Chairman of the Finance Committee, and the NDP was represented by the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) and myself.
The stage is set. The national political party representatives go head to head in a test to solve our country's economic problems. The Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) becomes the Prime Minister and immediately he and his Tory colleagues enter into a sweetheart alliance with the Liberals to form a coalition government against the NDP. The NDP immediately embarks on a comprehensive program bringing business, labour, and government together in a new era of co-operation. We presented solutions and alternatives that were heralded as nothing short of brilliant. However, just as we were about to achieve economic and financial success, the Prime Minister, the former President of the Treasury Board, announces that he has bankrupted the federal treasury-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF DEFENCE CAPABILITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a saying that the price of peace is eternal vigilance. There are groups in Canada who think our present equipment for maintaining that vigil is not adequate. Surely there is no group more qualified to judge the merits of our military organization than our war veterans as represented by the Royal Canadian Legion. On behalf of that group and other concerned Canadians I would like to add my support to their requests for an immediate review of our defence capabilities.
The Royal Canadian Legion, in a letter to me this month, invited me to share with the House their concern that the Armed Forces at this time are extremely undermanned and lacking in modern arms and equipment. As well, they are deeply worried that we may not be able to meet future obligations with regard to defence. 1 submit that these concerns are real and valid, and that the Minister of Defence (Mr. Blais) should give serious consideration to the representations 1 have mentioned. With recent events giving tragic proof of the hostile intentions of the U.S.S.R., there is an urgent need to attend to the security of our country.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION POSSIBLE APPLICATION FOR CHANGE IN TELEPHONE TARIFFS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION POSSIBLE APPLICATION FOR CHANGE IN TELEPHONE TARIFFS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the moment Bell Canada and all other Canadian telephone companies charge their subscribers a fixed monthly rate for the right to make as many local calls as they want. Although a high percentage of households are quite comfortably able to pay for flat rate service, basic rate make a private phone for some Canadians prohibitively expensive. For this reason, apparently, the phone companies are continuing to consider introducing usage sensitive pricing, or local measured service, in which local calls would be billed according to one or more of the following factors: the number of calls, their duration, the time of day, and the distance.
If low income households use the phone sparingly, as the theory goes, then under usage sensitive pricing their phone
Oral Questions
bills could be much lower than under the present flat rate service.
My concern is that usage sensitive pricing will not provide less expensive phone service to the elderly and the poor since they have a greater need to use their phones as a vehicle to keep in touch with relatives and friends, to seek employment, and so on. Therefore I feel that extensive research should be done by the CRTC before it considers any application by Bell Canada to use the USP system, in order to ensure that the poor and the elderly will have adequate telephone facilities at a price they can afford.

subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONALITY OF PROPOSED BRITISH COLUMBIA LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice. It is clear that the Government of British Columbia intends to go ahead with its highly repressive legislation. Bill-2 currently before the British Columbia Legislature so restricts the right to organize, and the freedom of association as to be in clear violation of two international treaties signed by the Government of Canada, one in 1935 and one in 1948. Has the Government of Canada officially pointed this out to the Premier of British Columbia? Has it made an
September 21, 1983

official request, either for fundamental change in this legislation or for its complete withdrawal?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the legislation presently before the Legislature of British Columbia has concerned the federal Government in a number of ways. A number of individual Ministers, depending upon their responsibilities, have made representations to the Government of British Columbia, some by telegram. At the conference on human rights a week or two ago, I spoke about our concern that the human rights code would eliminate all the mediatory aspects and leave merely the legal skeleton, which is an enormous step backward. This Government is making its views known to the Government of British Columbia. Of course the legislative process is under way in that Province and there may very well be changes to that legislation in the course of its consideration there.

Is it prepared to show as a Government that it is as concerned about the civil liberties of people in the Province of British Columbia as it is about the civil liberties of people in the Province of Quebec?

It would not be appropriate for the Government of Canada to take any form of legal action in the courts until the legislation was actually in effect. In that case, of course, what we did was to intervene on behalf of groups in the Province that were appealing.

Madam Speaker, we are asking for some public and serious initiatives before the legislation takes effect. I come back to my first question to the Minister of Justice. Is the Minister aware that Bill-2 in the Province of British Columbia, which is currently being debated, violates at least two international agreements signed by the Government of Canada, one in 1935 and one in 1948? Minister agrees there is such a violation, why does the Government of Canada not approach, directly and officially, the Government of British Columbia and ask for changes in that legislation?

Member that we will be discussing the legislation which is before the British Columbia Legislature.

subsubtopic: LEBANON-ASSISTANCE FOR VICTIMS OF FIGHTING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Minister knows that we are all distressed by the daily news of tragic events taking place in Lebanon, and the Minister is also aware that we are in favour of the withdrawal from Lebanese territory of all foreign troops and armed factions, and that we want to help the Lebanese and their Government to establish their country's sovereignty over all Lebanese territory.

Has the Government made its position clear on the tragic events which are occurring in Lebanon? What is being done to assist those Lebanese who are suffering most as a result of the fighting?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just a few days ago I had the opportunity to meet with representatives of the Lebanese community in Canada. I expressed to them, as I do today, the distress we feel at the continued violence and fighting in Lebanon. We have consistently urged that all forces withdraw from Lebanon. We have supported the present Government in its efforts at reconciliation, and we have consistently supported the independent and territorial integrity of Lebanon. Obviously we regret that the mediation efforts under way have not been successful.

speechtext:
1 would ask, Madam Speaker, that the remaining questions be allowed to stand.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reasons for recommending, debating and making suggestions related to the motion are quite obvious. I would like to take the opportunity today to expound upon them. Unemployment, as we all know today, is our number one problem, and international trade plays an important factor relating to that problem. In fact, according to statistics provided by both the Canadian and the U.S. Governments, for every $1 billion in trade, approximately 25,000 new

September 21, 1983
Relations with Taiwan
Canadian jobs are created. Unfortunately, unlike most other countries, Canada has not reached its full potential for a variety of reasons, one of them concerning Taiwan.
Taiwan has the fastest growing economy in the world today. Although not recognized diplomatically by many nations including Canada, virtually all non-communist industrialized countries have established some form of bilateral nondiplomatic presence with Taiwan for the sake of promoting trade, but Canada has not. Canada, along with Italy, stands virtually alone in not taking advantage of the tremendous trade potential that exists between the two countries. That is why, for example, in 1982 Canada had a trade deficit with Taiwan of $363 million and a total trade figure of only $900 million. I say "only $900 million", because if one compares the trade figures with, let us say, the United States, the difference is staggering. We are speaking of $900 million worth of trade in Canada, whereby in 1982 the United States' trading figures with Taiwan amounted to over $15 billion. Japan, Germany, Australia and other industrialized nations are also far ahead of us. The reasons are simple. These countries, although they do not recognize Taiwan diplomatically, realize the importance of not shutting out a country whose economic growth is so far ahead of Mainland China, for example, that the per capita income in the last ten years increased by some 500 per cent in Taiwan, while communist China remained constant at approximately $400 U.S. per year per capita. It is difficult to comprehend, therefore, why we in this country not only do not promote trade with Taiwan but, in fact, create obstacles that prevent improved trade relations.
Of course, a glaring example is the visa situation. It is very difficult and inconvenient for businessmen, and in fact anyone travelling between the two countries, to obtain visas. A Taiwanese businessman wishing to come to Canada must fly to Hong Kong and apply for a visa through the Canadian High Commission there, usually with lengthy waiting periods.
In fact, Mr. Ken McGillvery, a Canadian group organizer living in Taipai, writes:
Canadians in Taiwan are irked by the present uncomfortable and sometimes offensive treatment we receive from the Canadian High Commission in Hong Kong. We have almost exhausted our patience and lost nearly all our confidence through experiences in recent years. The High Commission in Hong Kong has repeatedly made their attitude clear that Canadians living in Taiwan are a nuisance to them and they just wish that we did not exist. We get no service at all in the form of information or even a suggestion of concern for Canadian interests here. There is no channel to which we can turn should we need protection, legal advice or assistance. All these fundamental flaws of policy and administration are the making of the External Affairs Department as interpreted by the Canadian High Commission in Hong Kong.
Mr. McGillvery goes on to say:
Chinese nationals from Taiwan are singled out for insulting and often degrading treatment by petty 'secretaries' in the Hong Kong High Commission.
Businessmen have frequently been given a one-month visa after many delays when they have needed much longer to properly complete their essential business.
Those are comments from a Canadian living in Taiwan who sees firsthand some problems that Canadians and Taiwanese
businessmen who want to do business with Canada face under these conditions.
On the other hand, Canadians wanting to travel to Taiwan, of whom there are many, must apply for visas in the United States. In fact, last year 6,000 visas were issued to Canadians travelling to Taiwan. They must apply for these visas in the United States because they cannot do so in Canada. This procedure is not only costly in terms of money but, more important to a businessman, in terms of time. Canadian businessmen deserve better. We as Parliamentarians owe it to our business community to improve this situation and we need not look further than the United States for an example.
Although the Americans do not recognize Taiwan diplomatically, as we do not, Americans can obtain their visas in many major U.S. cities such as Chicago, Boston, New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, just to name a few. The Taiwanese can have their visas processed in Taiwan at the U.S. office called the American Institute in Taiwan.
That brings me to another crucial problem facing Canadian businessmen which is, as I said earlier, that Canada is virtually alone in not having an office in Taiwan for the benefit of promoting trade, facilitating the growth of commercial, cultural and other forms of non-diplomatic contact between the people of Canada and Taiwan and generally assisting Canadians visiting Taiwan both on business and pleasure.
Why is it that other countries have taken steps for their own benefit without, I emphasize, any major repercussions from communist China while Canada is again losing out in this regard? It is not only the United States which has established these non-diplomatic relations with Taiwan while holding diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China at the same time. Other countries include New Zealand, Great Britain, West Germany, France, Greece, Japan, Australia, Austria, Argentina, Brazil, Spain, Sweden, Belgium, Switzerland, and the list goes on. All have some form of a bilateral, non-diplomatic contact between their two countries for the benefit of their respective businesses, economies and peoples.
Yet with these and other obstacles in the way, 1 am pleased to announce today that a delegation of businessmen from Taiwan led by Mr. Vincent Siew, Director General of the Board of Foreign Trade in Taiwan, will be signing contracts for the purchase of over $150 million worth of Canadian goods and products later this year. The delegation of 14 business representatives is scheduled to arrive in Toronto on November 9 for a 15-day visit, which will include stopovers in Sudbury, Ottawa, Saskatoon, Vancouver and, of course, Toronto. They will purchase such diversified products as wheat, potassium chloride, coal, sulphur, and nickel while at the same time looking at such potential requirements as our high-tech industry, communications, transportation and so on, all of which can be sold to Taiwan with just a little bit of co-operation and encouragement.
This gesture of goodwill by the Taiwanese business community obviously goes a long way toward reducing the trade deficit with that country. But it is just a drop in the bucket

compared to the potential that exists. It is up to us to take the necessary steps to be able to reach that potential.
An obvious example of that potential, other than the areas 1 have mentioned, is the Candu. As everyone knows, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is experiencing serious difficulties due to the lack of orders. As a result, jobs are being lost and others are in jeopardy. In a recent report, Andrew Horvat, a Southam News reporter in Taipai, stated:
Taiwan's Power Corporation has been begging Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. to sell it a pair of reactors, but AECLs answer has been a consistent "no Candu", even though it would inject more than a billion dollars into the comatose Canadian nuclear industry.
In fact, Taiwan requires an 8,000 megawatt production in the next 15 years. That is seven times more than the James Bay project alone. They want our Candus, and they are willing to comply by any or all international safety and other regulations, as they in fact do with the U.S., France and others from whom they are currently purchasing nuclear reactors. In fact, there is a trial Candu reactor in Taiwan which is under the control of the United States. Yet we refuse to sell them more Candus even though the sale of each Candu would inject $1 billion into our economy and create 25,000 new jobs in Canada.
Under these economic conditions and with the unemployment level which exists in this country, surely some of these options should be considered by Parliament. 1 understand the sensitivity of having our Government deal directly with that of Taiwan, but this does not have to be the case. Atomic Energy could negotiate with the Taiwan Power Corporation or, if need be, through a third intermediary such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. In fact, it is precisely such an organization that could establish itself in Taiwan as a non-diplomatic office serving Canadians in processing visas in conjunction with the High Commission in Hong Kong. But they need some encouragement from this Parliament.
In fact, whether it is the Chamber of Commerce or some other organization, it could be structured along the lines of the American Institute in Taiwan. The AIT is a non-profit organization licensed in the District of Columbia and established for the purpose of carrying out U.S. transactions in Taiwan. As a result of that office the Americans are benefiting from the tremendous growth that is taking place in that country.
The time is long overdue for Canada to do the same as the United States and the other countries I have mentioned instead of continuing to miss the boat and these great opportunities, as we are currently doing, while other industrialized nations are taking full advantage of the economic phenomenon that is taking place in Taiwan.
These are just some of the things that this motion which we are debating today recommends. At the outset you read the motion, Mr. Speaker, but let me repeat it very briefly. Its purpose is for the Government to consider facilitating:
-the growth of commercial, cultural and other forms of contact between the people of Canada and Taiwan through (a) the establishment of a bilateral, non-diplomatic presence between Canada and Taiwan, including the issuance of visas directly in Taiwan and Canada thereby adopting the practice of Japan, the United States and most other western industrialized nations (b) the enhance-
Relations with Taiwan
ment of trade links between Canada and Taiwan, including (i) the encouragement of export trade by Canada to Taiwan through the granting of credits and other forms of support to Canadian businessmen (ii) the establishment of direct air links between Canada and Taiwan-
-(iii) the adoption of any other practical mechanism to encourage industrial and other non-diplomatic contact between Taiwan and Canada.
Having said that, I want to emphasize that in no way are we suggesting getting embroiled in a diplomatic situation. We do not have to get embroiled in a diplomatic situation. We recognize Taiwan diplomatically. We are suggesting that we take full advantage of the opportunities that exist in Taiwan.
I know the thrust of this motion is supported by many Members on both sides of the House. In fact, the motion was drafted earlier this year by members of the Canada-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Committee, of which there are 60 or 70 bipartisan Members of this House and of the other place.
Let me reiterate that what we are recommending is not new from an international standpoint. It is not a precedent-setting idea, far from it. I will repeat again, because I have to, that what is being suggested is for Canada to follow the lead of most other non-communist industrialized nations. These nations, which took positive steps before we did, continue to build and to enjoy diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China without any loss of face or trade potential, whatever it is worth, yet their economies grow as a result of their increased trade with Taiwan.
We believe that, should measures of this nature be adopted for Canada, it would lead toward realizing and utilizing the full potential that exists, a potential able to create tens of thousands of jobs in Canada and that would inject billions of dollars of much needed capital into our economy. To this end we urge the Government to join virtually all other non-communist industrialized nations in establishing a non-diplomatic presence in Taiwan so as to take full advantage of the tremendous trade potential for the benefit of all Canadians.

products. The proposal in question would help countries in the south to raise their standards of living and to buy goods from the north. It would also promote the creation of jobs here in Canada. To get back to Taiwan and the kind of country it is, I would say that it is a democracy. I visited that country and saw its industry and its people, I asked a lot of questions, and I had a lot to think about. When visiting that country, we realize that its people have an enormous will to succeed, to make their way in the world and to get their own place in the sun, and that they are very hard workers. They are good workers in industry but also in their schools and universities, because the level of education is rising very rapidly, a sign of considerable ambition. This eagerness to work and to study has, as my colleagues mentioned earlier, resulted in a very substantial increase in the standard of living of the people of Taiwan. At first, the country had trouble even feeding its people, and today, the people are not only being fed but offered the luxury of having better doctors, improved medical care, and a better education, and I think this is a trend we Canadians would agree is a fortunate one that we would like to see in all countries throughout the world.
It is sometimes difficult for us Canadians to promote trade with Taiwan, because the situation is somewhat tense between Communist China and that country. However, when we are doing business, do we have to go into all the differences that often exist between the people of a country who have gone their separate ways? Today, we are selling a host of goods to the USSR, and I have no objection to that, although I am sure that many Canadians do not agree with the political system in that country. However, whatever the Soviet political system may be to us, we are selling them wheat, raw materials and many kinds of finished products, while they are selling us cars and a number of other commodities. So in the case of China and Taiwan, I think we should let those countries settle their own differences. They are mature people who are capable of governing themselves. However, we, as the Canadian Government, must take advantage of the opportunities we are offered and sell as many products as we can to this country. In fact, today, and it has been the case for many years, Taiwan exports a large number of products to Canada, and all consumers in the House or in the visitors' gallery will certainly agree with me that we see a lot of items made in Taiwan in the stores. Other countries, very important countries such as the United States, Japan, France, Germany and most industrialized countries have solved this problem. They have not officially recognized Taiwan at the diplomatic level, but they have sent commercial attaches there in order to promote trade, and

when we promote trade, it very often works out to the advantage of both countries.

at the end of the Chamber stand. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville, whom I remember meeting after a visit to communist China, would give us the benefit of some of his ideas as a result of visiting that country and tell us how well off the people were, as he saw during his travels.

Member for Halton pointed out that in ten years Taiwan has increased the level of income by 500 per cent, while in

subsubtopic: STUDY ON ECONOMIC IMPACT OF DELAY IN ALSANDS AND IMPERIAL OIL PROJECTS
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for copies of all papers and studies done for any department or agency concerning the economic impact to Canada of a one-year delay in the development of the Alsands project in Fort McMurray, Alberta and the Imperial Oil project in Cold Lake, Alberta.
He said: Mr. Speaker, 1 think anyone familiar with my activities in this House, particularly as they relate to the national energy policy and the resulting destruction of the tar sands and oil industry situated in my riding, will understand, when reading the order I have put forward, that I ask for

September 21, 1983
Energy
copies of all papers and studies done by any department or agency concerning the economic impact on Canada of a one-year delay in the development of the Alsands project in Fort McMurray and the oil sands project of Imperial Oil in Cold Lake. This was done on December 22, 1982. At that time, if you will remember, the announcements coming out of northeastern Alberta were pretty much gloom and doom as they relate to the oil sands industry. Alsands had announced its consortium had collapsed and it was not going to proceed with the $12 billion project. At approximately the same time it was announced that the Imperial Oil project in my riding was not going to be proceeded with.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, statements were made by the Alsands consortium and Imperial Oil which indicated these projects were not economically viable, but always with the proviso that this was so because of the present fiscal regime existing in the national energy policy, particularly the petroleum gas revenue tax. That tax represented a massive grab from these very sensitive and very marginal operations, taking money from the investors and the production at a time when it was risky business to develop these projects. Indeed, in some ways it is still a risky business to develop them.
The Alsands project presents a massive infusion of capital to buy the equipment and machinery, to build the complex necessary to mine the sands because in the open-pit mining process there are vast amounts of overburden which have to be removed in order to get at the oilsands. Syncrude and Suncor are doing this now. It is remarkable to note that 20 years ago Suncor went into that very speculative venture, the mining of the oil sands, to develop a process for extraction and upgrading of this very heavy bitumen into a very high quality synthetic crude. In fact, it is of such high quality that it is in demand virtually everywhere.
Learning from the experience of the Great Canadian Oil Sands plant, which later became Suncor, Syncrude went into developing a project which cost $9 billion. Again learning from their predecessor across the road, they developed and are now producing probably twice the capacity of the Suncor plant. The reason I am giving you the background on this, Mr. Speaker, is that I want everyone to understand that the Economic Council of Canada indicated two years ago in a study that $260 billion must be spent between now and 1990 if Canada is to reach oil self-sufficiency. Remember that at that time there was also the fight over the energy agreement between the Province of Alberta and the federal Government. When it was struck, the petroleum gas revenue tax included in the new national energy policy was so devastating that both Alsands and Imperial Oil at Cold Lake said no, we cannot risk $12 billion to invest in these massive projects because of the massive tax grab by the federal Government. That is in effect what they say.
Now, the Minister of Energy at that time and the Minister of Energy (Mr. Chretien) today will deny this. The various Parliamentary Secretaries and Liberal backbenchers will all deny this. They say it costs too much, it is inflation, interest rates. They go through all of that, but when you come to the
bottom line the companies themselves state that the PGRT was too big a bite and it now becomes too risky.
What was being risked, Mr. Speaker? Let us look at Imperial Oil. We were asking Imperial Oil, with a total capitalization in Canada of less than $ 12 billion, to gamble all of its assets in Canada on one plant in Cold Lake. That is what it amounted to. The mining of the oil sands in the Cold Lake area is different from that in Fort McMurray because it is not strip mining. There are various methods they are trying to develop such as drilling holes and pumping gas or hot water to heat the sands and then pump up the crude. The overburden is much too heavy or thick to remove.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a giant research and development project. Not only does it create jobs and contribute to our energy security and our balance of payments because we replace offshore oil with that from the oil sands, but it is developing technology which is needed in places like Venezuela which also has oil sands. I had a discussion with the Ambassador from Venezuela the other night. When he heard that I was from the riding of Athabasca he immediately recognized that as the area where research and development was taking place which he and his countrymen are very interested in. But we must consider the costs and the recovery of those costs is enhanced when a plant like this goes ahead.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that some Member from the Liberal side is going to stand today and say that the plants, these megaprojects, are dead, they are too expensive, or that the Hon. Member for Athabasca knows full well that the cost of oil was dropping and therefore they could not recover their investment and they became too risky. Before those statements are made, Mr. Speaker, I would only say that that is balderdash because the companies clearly indicate in press releases that it was the fiscal regime put in place by the federal Government which made the venture too risky.
Surprisingly enough, yesterday in Calgary the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, with the Minister of Energy for Alberta, announced that new life is being breathed into the Imperial Oil Project at Cold Lake. In the official press release from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources Canada, the Minister noted, "At the peak of the construction, 700 direct jobs will be created and will be filled primarily by residents of the Cold Lake region. Another 90 permanent jobs will result from the operational phase of the project. Three hundred million dollars is being invested for 700 construction jobs and 90 permanent jobs." What was originally proposed at Cold Lake was a project which, at peak construction, would provide 7,500 jobs, which would translate into 3,000 permanent jobs, from one plant alone. Double the figure, because the same type of investment was to be made north of Fort McMurray with the Alsands project. Can one imagine the effect there would be on the economy of the country today, the effect on the unemployment figures of 1.5 million people, had those two plants been allowed to continue? The unemployment figure would have been reduced by at least 500,000 to 700,-

September 21, 1983
000. That would be the impact of those two plants across Canada. It would have created an economic stimulus in Ontario alone of close to $7 billion in continual spending over the life of the projects.
However, when one turns the press release over, there is one statement that really points to where the Government is at: "The federal Government will provide earned depletion allowance". That is one thing that the Government denied both plants. The Government said that one cannot have earned depletion allowance. It further states that there will be "a waiver of payment of the petroleum gas revenue tax until the company has recovered its capital cost in accordance with the federal budget provisions announced in April 1983". In other words, when both the Alsands consortium and the Imperial Oil project at Cold Lake were prepared to invest $12 billion in each plant, a total of $24 billion, the Government said, "No, you will not receive depletion allowance. Yes, you will pay petroleum gas revenue tax from the moment you start pumping oil into the pipeline". But now Imperial has come back, and to encourage Imperial to invest $300 million, which may develop into $1.5 billion over the next three years, the Government has done exactly what the oil companies and the heavy oil industry said needed to be done in the first place. 1 would suggest that it is exactly two years too late.
If the Government had not been so concerned with grabbing from the goose that was laying the golden egg, if it had not been so concerned that someone might make a dollar, there would be two plants in northeastern Alberta ready to come onstream, probably in 18 months, producing 280,000 barrels of oil per day, which would amount to approximately 14 per cent of our total national supply of oil. Employment would be created across Canada in virtually every Province amounting to over 500,000 jobs, and probably closer to 700,000 jobs. We would not be buying oil offshore. We are presently importing under 200,000 barrels a day and even paying spot prices in some cases which are higher than world prices, adding to our deficit in foreign trade, which affects the dollar and employment in a vicious cycle. We would have already saved at least $5 billion in unemployment insurance benefits that have been paid out because the jobs were not there. We would have saved untold misery across the country to those men and women who are unemployed and who have now exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits, those who have sold their homes, cars, personal belongings and have gone onto welfare. God only knows how much damage we would have saved the children who are witnessing traumatic kinds of confrontations that they have never before seen happening in their families. We do not have to be all that intelligent to understand what happens when a man walks into his home-or a woman-and sees children for which he cannot provide because he cannot find a job in a stagnant economy. It does not take much to imagine the kinds of things that go on in that home. It would have saved small companies and even larger companies. Tar Sands Machine and Welding was a company in Fort McMur-ray owned by an individual who had invested his time, his life savings, and who was doing a superb job in the heavy oil indus-
Energy
try. However, with the collapse of Alsands, of course, he collapsed. He had about 65 employees who all lost their jobs. I could recount numbers of different companies all over northeastern Alberta to which this happened primarily because the Government would not clear the smoke from its eyes. The Government was so concerned because it thought Alberta was being greedy and pitted the rest of the country against certain people in the oil industry in Alberta. This cash-starved Government was so concerned with grabbing as many dollars as possible, spending like a drunken sailor with no accountability to the House of Commons, that it killed two projects that are needed today as they were needed then and will be needed tomorrow for our own security. The security of our country is at stake because we do not have a secure supply of oil. Yet we have Petro-Canada, which receives a stipend from the Canadian taxpayer, investing $.5 billion in offshore China to develop oil reserves there.
When questioned as to why this is being allowed to happen, the answer comes back, "It will be a supply of oil for Canada". My God, we have reserves in the tar sands which surpass the known conventional reserves in the Middle East. We have an abundance of oil and we have the ability and technology to extract it from the tar sands. It could create jobs in Canada and thereby decimate the unemployment lines. It would keep dollars in Canada instead of their being spent offshore for oil. It would create a healthy economy. It would bind the country together because when there are jobs in northeastern Alberta, people would come from every Province to that area. God bless them for it because it creates a mix of Canadians in the region. When Hibernia finally develops people will migrate to the region from one end of the country to the other and there will be a mix. That is how we build a country.
My motion is very simple. 1 only want to see the papers and the studies that were done. To my knowledge, these studies were done and indicated to the Government and the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, before he brought down his National Energy Policy in Bill C-48, the drastic consequences if those plants did not come onstream. Yet he ignored it.
My final comment is that we were looking at an outside investment, not Government investment, of $24 billion. The Economic Council of Canada stated very clearly in their studies that $260 billion must be invested in the energy sector if we are to have energy self-sufficiency by the year 2000, not 1990.
I hope Hon. Members will join with me and force the Government to table these papers so that everyone in the House of Commons and all Canadians can see why and how the Government came to its decision with the petroleum gas revenue tax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to speak in this debate because it deals
27350

September 21, 1983
Energy
with what I believe is a very important question, oil sands development and particularly the Alsands project.
Before 1 commence with what I intend to say, let me suggest that the demagoguery of the Hon. Member who just spoke is just incredible. To suggest as he does that the federal Government alone is responsible for the fact that the Alsands project did not proceed is to continue in the same kind of demagoguery, and what I would characterize as garbage, that we hear from Members on that side of the House when it comes to energy issues. Whenever the federal Government becomes involved in policies on national issues, some Members, particularly in the Conservative Party, think that it is sacrilege.
The Hon. Member should know and have the honesty to tel! the public that the timing error for the Alsands project occurred when Premier Lougheed and his Government decided to use the Alsands project as a hostage in the negotiations for an oil pricing agreement. This was in the winter of 1980 and 1981, well before the Alsands project was finally cancelled by the companies involved after the very attractive offer both Governments made in the spring of 1982. That is when the mistake was made. It is unfortunate.
Premier Lougheed decided that this was one of the projects he would hold up. He could have found a fiscal regime in the fall of 1980 and winter of 1981 for the Alsands project. The federal Government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources at that time kept answering questions in the House and saying publicly that he was ready at any time to sit down to get an agreement on a fiscal regime with the Province of Alberta for the Alsands project. However, the Premier of Alberta decided that he would not have it so. That was well before the oil pricing agreement was arrived at in the beginning of September or end of August.
Premier Lougheed had used the Alsands project as a pawn in very tough negotiations. I am not saying he was wrong in using it that way because he is very effective at protecting the interests of his electorate. He made the political judgment that he would not let that project go ahead and would not negotiate the fiscal regime with the Government of Canada or with the companies before he had an oil pricing agreement. That is all right, but he made that decision, not the federal Government.
I distinctly recall the discussions we had in our caucus and the discussions that were held elsewhere when we were pleading with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to do more to ensure that the project would go ahead, because, as the Member said, it was not only very important in terms of energy supply, the security of supply for the future of Canada, but it was very important because of the industrial benefits it would have provided across the country. But the Alberta Government refused to negotiate a fiscal regime before there was an oil pricing agreement.
That error was made and it is unfortunate. We all know what occurred subsequently. As we got into 1982 the pricing situation became uncertain. Despite the very attractive offer on the part of both levels of Government, the companies decided not to proceed. At that time both Governments did all they could but unfortunately it was too late. The offer that was
presented jointly by both Governments first assured private sector participation would be at least 50 per cent, but in view of normal tax write-offs the two Governments would provide guarantees for 68 per cent of the private sector expenditures in the pre-production period. Second, no repayment of interest or principal would be scheduled until after start-up. Interest on the guaranteed loan could be capitalized and added to the oustanding loan balance and the guarantee increased accordingly. After production start-up, 58 per cent of the net revenue accruing to the private sector would be paid on the loan guarantees. Net revenue was equal to gross revenues minus 110 per cent of the operating costs, minus capital additions, minus the Alberta 5 per cent gross royalty.
I could go on, but I think it has all been said publicly already. The result was that private oil firms withdrew from the project despite the Government offer which would have removed a large part of the financial risk from the private investors. They would still have maintained 50 per cent private ownership. All told, the direct and indirect support by Canada and Alberta would have covered 84 per cent of the project costs then estimated at $13.9 billion. That was in 1982 and 1 suppose that investment would now be well over $14 billion.
The Hon. Member has talked about the petroleum gas revenue tax. Again, they consider it a sacrilege to have the federal Government raise a tax from the top. They say that is terrible because it goes directly at the cash flow. However, provincial royalties are taken directly from the top and that seems to be all right. Simply because the federal Government would decide to have a tax mechanism which takes money from the top, it is supposed to be bad. Apparently it is all right to be used as a policy instrument for provincial governments. 1 do not know how Hon. Members can reconcile that unless they only want to continue to oppose anything the federal Government does.
The PGRT would have become effective only after the guaranteed loans would have been repaid. The rate of tax would have been 16 per cent, but now, with changes that have been announced recently, would be less than that. Unless somebody opposes the PGRT for everything, which I know is the honest position of some of the Members, then one cannot say that the PGRT alone was the only reason this project did not go ahead. The PGRT would have become effective only after the guaranteed loans had been repaid.
I wanted to intervene briefly in this debate. As the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) said, it is a very important debate. I am happy now that some projects are going ahead. 1 am happy the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) has made sure that some changes to the fiscal regime have been made and that Petro-Canada as an instrument of public policy is involved in the Alsands development and in heavy oil. I believe this is important for the security of supply of energy in Canada. I believe it is important because of the industrial benefits which these massive projects will bring to the rest of the country.
September 21, 1983

As I have said, to suggest that the federal Government alone is responsible that the Alsands project did not go ahead, to use such language as to say the federal Government killed the Alsands project, is to hide from the truth. The time to go ahead with the Alsands project was the spring of 1981 or even in the fall of 1980. The construction of the projects would have been so far ahead that by the time the pricing situation became uncertain in the world it would have been too late for companies to cancel.
The fiscal benefits were always available from the federal Government. The federal Government was always ready, during 1981 and before that, to sit down with officials from the Province of Alberta and negotiate a regime. The Alberta Government refused to do that.

subsubtopic: STUDY ON ECONOMIC IMPACT OF DELAY IN ALSANDS AND IMPERIAL OIL PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on the motion for the production of papers concerning the economic impact of the delay of the Alsands project in Fort McMurray, Alberta and the Imperial Oil project in Cold Lake.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) blame the federal Liberals for the collapse of these megaprojects. The Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) condemned the provincial Conservatives in the Province of Alberta for the collapse of these oil projects. I must say that I agree with them both. Not only should the blame be placed upon them for the collapse of these projects, it should also be placed upon the resource giants.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Athabasca that the federal Liberals did not and do not understand the oil industry. As a result they tried to compromise and change their position on many occasions, but they were unsuccessful because of what I believe was a true lack of understanding about the industry.
I do not know why the Conservative Government under the leadership of Premier Lougheed in Alberta was so stubborn in the negotiations to push the projects ahead. They would have been meaningful to all Canadians and provided self-sufficiency in energy by the end of 1990, possibly even sooner. Could it have been that he was tied so closely to the resource companies that he could not allow the projects to go ahead? I do not know. That is a question which remains paramount in my mind.
Returning to the issue of laying blame, the resource giants involved in these megaprojects have always been guaranteed an annual income or income on every project in which they have become involved. The oil industry is a high-risk business. That risk is not only minimized to resource companies; it is almost eliminated. Unless the risk is eliminated they do not want to participate in the marketplace. They want to be guaranteed an annual return on each project in which they participate.
An as alternative to the squabbling which took place, there could have been some public intervention because of the large amount of taxpayer dollars which would have gone into these projects. Sometimes taxpayers receive a nil return in terms of compensation paid to resource companies for projects which did not go ahead. Millions of dollars would have been spent on these projects.
I am keenly interested in this notice of motion for the productions of papers concerning the economic impact of the delay in these projects because my constituency of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake is adjacent to the Alberta border. Many people across Canada, and particularly those in my riding, are affected by the economic benefits of these projects with large capital input into local areas. I know many people who work as labourers in the construction phases. Some small companies have been hurt badly by the collapse of the megaprojects on
September 21, 1983

which the Government relied heavily for creating employment and helping the economy of the country, projects which have now gone astray. Small companies working in the oilpatch were hit harder than others by the collapse of the megaprojects. These companies made plans to expand, to improve and to develop new services which could have been offered in support of the building of the projects. Their plans were ruined and some of them went bankrupt. Many individuals had problems with their families and their companies particularly as a result of the collapse of the Esso Resources project at Cold Lake. Small companies had made plans, worked on their budgets and knew what they would have to charge to make a living and to provide jobs and some security for their employees. Those which survived and remained in the marketplace after the collapse of the projects did so by working for whatever company offered them work.
I see Esso Resources will go ahead with the development at Cold Lake, albeit a much smaller project requiring much less capital and providing fewer jobs than was the case with the initial megaprojects. As was pointed out by an earlier speaker, the original proposal at Cold Lake included the spending of some $12 billion to $14 billion. Now that it is hopefully planned as a phased-in project, in the two initial phases there will be a capital cost of some $300 million or about 40 times less than originally intended.
It is interesting to note that megaprojects seem very efficient and seem to provide a large number of jobs. However, 1 would like to refer to the statistics of Esso Resources included in a book which 1 received on July 6, 1983. They indicate that although Esso is spending 40 times less money in the project at Cold Lake now, the number of jobs has not reduced correspondingly. For example, in the construction stage of the heavy oil plant the initial projection provided for some 8,000 to 10,000 new jobs. Now it will be between 400 and 700 jobs, somewhat under the 40 per cent less of the spending they are projecting. In terms of permanent jobs that will be created by this project, the original plans projected some 2,000 to 3,000 permanent jobs. With the reduced model and the phasing-in proposal, some 90 permanent jobs will be created in the Cold Lake project, again somewhat more corresponding to the 40 times less money they are spending.
The point I am making is that for the dollars spent, more jobs are being created for the people of Canada by Esso Resources phasing-in proposal than would have been created by the number of dollars spent in the large megaproject. I thought that was interesting to point out in the debate this afternoon.
It is significant to note that in the original proposal, it would have taken 10 to 12 years to complete the entire project. With the smaller version coming onstream, it will be four years. That is important because we need these jobs sooner, not later. The sooner we have those jobs, the better it will be for the people of that area as well as for people right across Canada.
Energy
There is something else that has not been mentioned this afternoon on which 1 would like to spend some time, namely the environmental concerns of people living in the project area. Although controls have been put in place and Esso Resources has gone through the proper hearings to have their project approved, 1 ask them publicly to be good corporate citizens as they go ahead with this project and to assure us that the environment that could be affected by such projects will be protected.
The first concern about the environment is the emission of sulphur dioxide, the main component in acid rain. My constituency of Meadow Lake is downwind. Prevailing winds blow from the Cold Lake project across the riding that ! represent, carrying the sulphur dioxide. This may cause future acid rain problems. The northern part of my riding is vulnerable to the effects of acid rain or acid precipitation because it is on the edge on the Pre-Cambrian Shield. The area does not have the ability to withstand the effects as do some agricultural areas to the south. Environment Canada operates an acid precipitation testing station at Cree Lake which monitors the situation very closely. If Esso Resources or any other resource giant is not a good corporate citizen and is not taking care of the environment, we will know that. We would then have to re-evaluate what they do in terms of polluting the environment. I again stress that I very much want them to be good corporate citizens.
There is a second area of environmental concern on which I have received numerous letters from the Village of Pierceland and the rural municipal council of Beaver River. Their concern is the water drained off Cold Lake and the placing of that waste, although will be treated, back into the river systems of the area. The Beaver River system, which runs through a good portion of my riding, affects such places as Goodsoil, Pierceland, Meadow Lake and places down the line. These people are justly concerned about the effects on their water supply and the ecosystems that could be affected by the waste material from the heavy oil plants. There could be an increase of the sewage effluent into the Beaver River system. They are also concerned about the possibility of ground water contamination due to a deep well disposal of waste from the steam injection process which may be used as well.
1 lodge with the House of Commons and my constituents my concern about what could happen to the environment. 1 am sure that all of us, including Esso Resources, do not want anything to happen to the environment. At the same time, 1 appreciate the economic activity created by the projects, creating jobs for many unemployed people, as pointed out by the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), not only in the immediate area but all across Canada. These people will go there to seek jobs and a new future with some stability of employment. There is a great deal of spin-off with small companies which service the resource giants, megaprojects and heavy oil projects. Providing jobs has the benefit of giving dignity to the people and makes their communities better places in which to live.

September 21, 1983
Energy
The only area of disagreement that 1 have with the motion is that I would like to see the tabling of the documents affecting the economy because of the delay in the project. If there are documents that are not public, and I hope the Hon. Member for Athabasca will agree with this, documents which affect environmental safety and the environmental consequences of the project going ahead, I would like to see them tabled in the House of Commons this afternoon. 1 appreciate the opportunity of being allowed to intervene in this debate.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DISHONOURED CHEQUES
speechtext:
that Bill C-574, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (n.s.f. cheques), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I feel personally compelled to thank my good friend, Mr. J. Larry Condon, the former Member for the Riding of Middlesex-London-Lambton, who spoke twice in support of my Bill since 1 was then holding the same position you are now holding, Mr. Speaker, and was prohibited from presenting and speaking on Bills.
I know that my former colleague, like all Members of the House, is very concerned about cheque frauds as it affects the consumer, who after all is the one who usually pays the shot because of increased prices of goods. As well, it affects the businessman who cannot afford to lose income because of n.s.f. cheques.
Many variety stores are now owned and operated by couples who have worked very hard at other jobs in order to save enough money to purchase a variety store. They do this so they can become independent and, by choice, work 14 to 16 hours a day in order to make less than a $12,000, $15,000 or $20,000 profit per year. In many cases these variety store owners have steady customers who pay in cash. However, the day comes when a customer is short of cash and the store operator in good faith accepts a cheque for goods purchased. If the cheque is returned marked "n.s.f.", the store operator does not have the time or money to hire a lawyer and lay a fraud charge which, I am told, is very hard to prove. The store operator absorbs the loss which is removed from his yearly profit.
No businessman, big or small, should be forced to take a customer to court to prove that that customer has attempted to defraud him. Surely the responsibility to make the cheque good within a reasonable period of time rests solely with the person who initially wrote the cheque.
This is why included in my Bill is the provision of a period of 15 days after notification by the bank in which to allow the person who wrote the cheque to avoid criminal liability by paying the debt off in full or by making the necessary arrangements to make restitution of the debt. In the event the debt is not paid off within that period, the defrauder would become liable to prosecution in the ordinary way.
September 21, 1983

This provision clearly places the responsibility on the shoulders of the person who has incurred the debt. In my opinion, the person who issued the cheque in the first place should be the one to prove that he was not trying to purchase goods by false pretence. If a person purchases goods by passing counterfeit bills or currency, is it not true that the police can be called and charges laid, Mr. Speaker? What is the difference between bad bills and bad cheques?
As an elected Member of Parliament for the riding of London East, I have for many years visited businessmen in their establishments who inform me that cheque fraud through the use of personal cheques has risen drastically during the past few years. Virtually every gas station, variety store, drugstore, etc., has displayed signs which point out that all services and merchandise must be paid for in cash, no cheques accepted. If the customer asks the proprietor why this is so, he or she will be shown a stack of n.s.f. cheques which have been passed to the merchant months or weeks before. This clearly indicates to me that something is wrong with our system.
For example, a furniture dealer recently advised me that he sold $3,000 worth of furniture to a customer and that furniture was paid for by cheque. The furniture was delivered the next day. The customer stopped payment on the cheque. To further make my point, another case involved gas stations that serviced trucks which hauled scrap metal from Windsor to Hamilton. At that time, some gasoline station owners allowed customers to pay their accounts by cheque. However, one of the drivers presented a $4,000 cheque to pay for the gas he had purchased with a credit card. The owner of the station got in touch with is customer's bank manager in Toronto who assured him that the account was good. A few days later, the cheque was returned n.s.f. The owner went to the police, to lawyers and to the courts and still received no justice because the incident was not considered to be one of obtaining goods by false pretence. I do not care what the lawyers say, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion, this method of business practice is totally dishonest and should not be tolerated.
It seems to me that the part of the Code under consideration, in its application and operation if not in its wording, puts Canadian businessmen and merchants through a great deal of unnecessary legal expense in an attempt to recover payment for bad cheques which were issued for nothing more than payment for goods owned by the merchants in the first place. The primary purpose of this Bill is to try to improve the present law so as better to protect the small businessmen, landlords and citizens who suffer most from receiving n.s.f. cheques. In the past, recipients of n.s.f. cheques have had no other recourse but to go to small claims court or the criminal law courts in an attempt to recover the money lost.
There are many good reasons for which people write bad cheques. In some cases, it is an honest error on the part of the drawer of the cheque, and in most instances he will redeem the worthless cheque promptly after notification that his cheque was dishonoured. In such cases, full payment or even an arrangement to pay on terms is sufficient evidence to indicate
Criminal Code
that the drawer of the cheque did not commit fraud as would otherwise appear to be the case.
During the past many years, those who have suffered most from n.s.f. cheques have been the small businessmen who on knowing the person and seeing that person-
