speechtext:
Thank you, Sir. I was just reading from a note.
As an example, a person who intends to rent an apartment often pays the rent in advance by writing three or four post-dated cheques. If the landlord advises the tenant that the first cheque has bounced, the tenant should have the idea that he will be put out on the street. However, due to the provisions of the Ontario Landlords and Tenants Act, he cannot be put out on the street during the months of October, November and December. This puts the landlord in the position of having to house the tenant for free. The landlord cannot collect the rent to which he is entitled without engaging in costly court proceedings. Usually he has to go to court.
Another vital problem we all find is when a person purchases goods. In the past, all governments have made an attempt to assist small businessmen and help them take the opportunity to expand and develop their businesses. But the latter has been restricted by the law under which it is possible for people to pay for their purchases by cheque. The small businessman depends on the local person to walk in, examine his goods and pay cash for the goods. This allows the business-

Criminal Code
man to buy more goods, thus creating more jobs in making his products. When he makes more sales this increases his assets, thus expanding his business.
I think we have a moral as well as a legal obligation to protect businessmen and workers, such as the Maislin workers who were issued cheques which the banks would not honour when the cheques were first presented to the banks. Many hard-working people have lost pay money when their pay cheques were marked "NSF" and the company had gone into receivership. Our criminal law provides no satisfaction for the merchant, the landlord or the worker because the law does not provide automatic repayment of n.s.f. cheques.
Let us be honest about this n.s.f. cheque law because the present law does not deter others from committing the same kind of crime. The law is viewed at the present time as a licence to steal from our businessmen. These same offenders walk down the street using the argument that "if 1 can beat the system and get away with it, why not?"
French law certainly treats this as an offence and the severity of the punishment depends solely on the amount of money involved. The fraud is considered very serious. If the n.s.f. cheque is between $200 and $700, the penalty is from one to five years and a fine between $720 and $7,200. Some residents of Canada may think that this is harsh but every Member of this House has heard of cases where five years would be too lenient in an n.s.f. cheque case. Surely, Mr. Speaker, our business people, merchants, landlords and workers should have the best protection of the law which would prevent financial suffering through the loss of hundreds of dollars each year. We have been told that all credit card companies suffer millions of dollars loss annually from people who work the system. I ask you, is it not true that if n.s.f. cheques and credit card frauds were eliminated by a tough law, our Canadian cost of products and living would drop drastically?
The only altenative to cash for consumers is the use of the credit card. The risk of this form of credit is assumed by the bank, oil company or department store which issues the card and the cost of that risk is paid by all customers whether they use such a card or pay cash.
Nor has the merchant been slow to see the use of credit cards. He has learned that credit customers purchase 33 per cent more than cash customers because credit customers, unlike those who write personal cheques, are not compelled to determine whether or not they can cover the cost of the purchase from their available funds. Is it not correct to assume that credit card customers are merely putting a mortgage on their future income? Therefore, for the sake of counterfeit cheque writers, we are forcing the ordinary consumer to purchase on credit, to become a debtor, and too often a bad debtor who gets in debt over his head and loses everything. Is this what we want or are we prepared to put some larger and stronger teeth into the present law against cheque frauds before cheques disappear altogether?
Banks are endeavouring to get all their customers to use their new electronic machines, but recently we have been
September 21, 1983
advised by the news media that fraud artists have been taking money out of these machines from customers' accounts. In Vancouver recently $800 was taken in this way.
No matter how we look at the offence, or whatever the amount of the cheque, the elements of the offence are the same. First, issuance of the cheque; second, lack of funds at the moment of issue; and third, bad faith of the author of the cheque.
Just what is bad faith, you might ask. Bad faith does not suppose even the intention to cheat or defraud. It does not necessarily mean that the person who wrote the cheque knew there were insufficient funds. French courts assume that a person writing a cheque has a duty-and, Mr. Speaker, I agree-to know the state of his account, and therefore bad faith may be proven in the case of a person who, in doubt of his situation, writes a cheque without taking the precaution of verifying the state of his account. I do not think that is too hard to accept.
In France if the amount involved is less than $200, the offence is considered a breach of regulations. Not only is the punishment less severe, but the bad cheque speaks for the bad faith of the author of the cheque and off he goes to jail for writing a cheque without checking his bank balance. Mr. Speaker, this places the responsibility where it belongs-right on the cheque writer.
I understand that penal legislation concerning cheques is often temporarily altered because the courts are clogged with writers of n.s.f. cheques waiting for their turn in jail. If there is a surplus of n.s.f. cases, a period of ten days is allowed the author of the bad cheque from the time of the issuance of the cheque, during which he could make repayment. Thus a person who pays up is able to escape jail but is still liable to the payment of the fine. By contrast, Bill C-574 allows the cheque counterfeiter and any bad bookkeeper alike 15 days to pay what is owed, as evidence that they did not obtain something of value under false pretences. Anyone who believes that this treatment is too harsh should state why a Canadian crook deserves better treatment than a French fraud artist.
For the sake of the consumer in the marketplace and every merchant with whom he deals and who could, if he was not defrauded by these sharp cheque operators, lower the price of his saleable goods, I strongly suggest that there is a great need for a plain and simple Canadian law. It should identify and eliminate cheque counterfeiters and allow the police to bring about the evidence and allow prosecution by the Crown without requiring the businessman, the merchant, the landlord, or the little fellow in business, to weigh the cost and the benefit of trying to collect payments on account of bad cheques.
Let us as Canadians give the Canadian businessman the protection he justly deserves-the elimination of taking the n.s.f. cheque artist to court to collect his money if he can place the responsibility solely on the cheque artist and make him pay his bills or serve the consequences in jail or pay a heavy fine.
In my view the proposed Bill would provide and update such a law. I heartily support it and suggest that the Bill be passed
September 21, 1983

and that Hon. Members agree the subject matter be referred to the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DISHONOURED CHEQUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to my friend, the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Turner), 1 am not too sure what side of the question he is on. His whole speech-which he read-inveighed against the bad cheque writer and all the harm he does. Yet the amendment that was proposed would open the gates to far more cheque fraud.
I do not know what the Hon. Member is driving at. When an offence is committed by the issuance of a cheque for which there are no funds or not sufficient funds, the police recognize the difficulty of successful prosecution, particularly where small amounts are involved. There must be an intent to commit fraud. Then if the payee temporizes with the fraudulent payor by an extension of time to pay the cheque, that converts it into a commercial debt and there is no more criminal element to it. That is the difficulty.
Subsection 320(1) of the Criminal Code provides:
Every one commits an offence who (a) by a false pretence, whether directly or through the medium of a contract obtained by a false pretence, obtains anything in respect of which the offence of theft may be committed or causes it to be delivered to another person;-
You can commit a theft with regard to money or goods; you cannot commit a theft of services. It goes on:
(b)	obtains credit by a false pretence or by fraud;-
That is the person who fails to pay his hotel account or his motel account, and I look here at my good friend, the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass). It continues:
(c)	knowingly makes or causes to be made, directly or indirectly, a false statement in writing with intent that it should be relied upon-
Well, one can almost get into a cheque there, but let us go down to the reference to obtaining delivery of personal property. Well, that is a suit. The payment of money, yes. Go into a bank, credit union or what have you and obtain some money by issuing a bad cheque. I can commit an offence by writing a cheque for which there are insufficient funds and giving it to a person who has sought a loan from me. Instead of giving that person cash I give them a cheque for which there are not sufficient funds. That is to establish the debt. There may be some money in the account, but if I issue a cheque for $1,000 because a friend asks me for a loan of $1,000, I enter into a contract with him that he owes me $1,000 on a particular date. Then he cannot obtain any money for it so there is a false pretence.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the discount of an account receivable. Oh, that is a good one! My friend, the Hon. Member for London East, must know that in dealing particularly with small service businesses quite often individuals will run up accounts. They may owe $75 and they come along and say to the chap: "If you will take $60 I will give you a cheque for it; give me a discount." That is a false pretence.
Criminal Code
Then there is the making, accepting, discounting or endorsing of a bill of exchange, cheque, draft or promissory note. That is the narrow application the Hon. Member wishes to consider in this Bill. This would be an indictable offence and that is serious. The person would be liable to imprisonment for ten years.
It has been my experience, Mr. Speaker, that this business of writing bad cheques means a loss either to the bank, the credit union or the cheque cashing agency if they are unable to charge it back to the payee of the cheque or the person who deposits the cheque in an account. Such cases run into the millions of dollars. If you are going to be so solicitous of the so-called little guy, giving him an extra 15 days to make good his cheque, what about the professional swindler who is a real bouncer of cheques? He is long gone at the end of 15 days. In this day and age an individual could go around bouncing cheques here in Ottawa to the tune of several thousands of dollars, and if my friend's amendment were to go through, which I hope it will not, nor even be considered any further with all due respect, the victim could find out the cheque was bad the same day or the next morning and yet according to this amendment there would be 15 days' grace after which a charge could be laid if the cheque were still unpaid. Well, in this day and age I think I could be lost in the Himalayas within 15 days. I could be in the centre of Africa or up the Amazon River in the jungle. In other words, absolutely long gone and no one could reach me because of this amendment. So 1 do not see it at all.
Where there is a bad cheque from an individual who rents a room, an apartment or a house, there is a small debt court available. No one is going to tell me that is a very difficult procedure. There are no lawyers, the fees are very low and that is recoverable as a civil debt. There is no criminal charge involved.
1 think my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), who has had years of experience as a Crown prosecutor, knows that the police are very chary of persons who, in laying complaints about bad cheques, are trying to use the criminal court as a collection agency. Therefore, they say: "Go to the small debt court," because it is so very difficult to prove that at a certain instant there was not sufficient money. If there was sufficient money in the account at the time the cheque was written, that is a defence. If the individual who wrote the bad chque expected to receive money which he or she could deposit in the account to cover the particular cheque that was being written, that is a defence.
However, in this day and age of less than the Pony Express for a Post Office, there is a very serious situation concerning cheques on which people rely. How many people receive their monthly pension cheque, dividend cheque or retirement cheque by post with varying degrees of deliverability? They have issued cheques to their landlords for utilities and what have you.

Therefore, this question involving cheque fraud is a very serious one. Both are defences and the Act already provides for those and for small debt action. Therefore, I do not see what the benefit of the amendment would be, with all due respect to the Hon. Member for London East, but it is an open sesame for the professional cheque bouncer, the fraud artist. Lord only knows the untold millions of dollars that are fleeced each year here in Canada and in the United States.
I know that the judges in the United States take a much tougher view concerning bad cheques than they do here in Canada. I know of many cases of Alberta citizens who were caught somewhere down in the States bouncing cheques, and not necessarily big ones, perhaps a few hundred dollars, and they finished up doing five years at McNeil Island. They were as regular as clockwork. Five years seemed to be about the minimum sentence for a cheque involving $300 or $400. That may be a little strong but, on the other hand, it is still a penalty.
I do not agree with the purport of the amendment. I would therefore ask the House to talk it out or reject it.

speechtext:
Police forces must spend more time investigating serious criminal activities such as assaults, child abuse, outright business frauds, and driving under the influence of alcohol or other drugs. The sentences should reflect the seriousness of such crimes. At the same time, people should no longer be sent to jail for petty crimes and minor offences. In those cases, the sentences are costlier than the crimes and the taxpayers have to pick up the tab.

This is a very good Bill. It is a short Bill. It is a modest Bill. It is such an excellent idea that I wonder why it has not been thought of before. It does two things at the same time. First, it actually encourages people to honour their debts, their bad cheques.
I think the remarks of the previous Conservative speaker were quite fanciful. The possibilities he mentioned were extremely remote concerning professional criminals taking advantage of an amendment of this sort. As a professional sociologist and criminologist, 1 can tell the House that a far more likely occurrence would be that a large number of lesser criminals or people who, through some error, have given out

September 21, 1983

cheques without adequate funds in the bank would in fact pay up. It would mean that people would be paid. The real victims, small family companies, variety stores, the sort of people who very much miss the money denied to them as a result of bad cheques, would be helped by the amendment before us today.
The second reason I support this amendment is that it attempts to scale down the criminal law in the non-violent area. We have a criminal law in Canada which has very repressive means of enforcement. This means that many people go to jail for trivial and non-violent offences for which the taxpayers must pay enormous costs. There are people who go to jail in some cases for theft of a dollar or very trivial amounts of money. It costs up to $75 a day, depending upon the institution. It costs enormous amounts of money to keep them in prison. It is a stupid way to run a system.
There are people who are real victims, such as battered wives, abused children and the many people who are hit by impaired drivers on the road. They are the real victims of violence and do not receive the attention they need in the criminal justice system because it is going after many smaller offenders. There needs to be a fine-tuning of the system with greater severity where there are real dangers and less severity where the dangers are not so great.
I suggest that we ought to pass this Bill today. While we will be seeing far more comprehensive amendments, like comprehensive amendments everywhere they take longer to pass and who knows when we will be actually seeing them. While I want more comprehensive amendments to the Criminal Code, I am quite prepared to support any good measure that is introduced in the meantime. Let us take a step in the right direction and pass this Bill this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 share the difficulty that the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has in seeing how this Bill would produce the effect hoped for by the Member for London East (Mr. Turner). 1 agree with him when he says that this amendment would in all likelihood open the gates to far more cheque fraud and therefore have the opposite effect from that intended by the Hon. Member for London East.
In his comments he drew to the attention of the House that the use of cheque fraud has increased in recent years. He referred to the plight of many variety store owners and the fact that many gas stations today do not accept cheques because of difficulties that have occurred in the past. He said that this proposal would place responsibility where it belongs, on the cheque writer. Again, I have difficulty in seeing how this would happen.
It seems to me that his proposal would have a contrary effect. At the present time, an offence under Section 320 is committed when a person purchases goods or offers in payment a cheque which he knows to be worthless. Some of us have had the opportunity to study law. We know what the
Criminal Code
concept of mens rea, or a guilty mind, is about. To be guilty of an offence under many sections of the Criminal Code, one has to know that one is committing a crime at the time it is being committed. It used to be very difficult to obtain a conviction under these circumstances with this particular section of the Criminal Code because it was necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused knew that there were not sufficient funds in his account at the time he gave the cheque. That is obviously a very difficult thing to do.
An ordinary citizen who normally has a couple of hundred dollars in an account may issue a cheque, as we all do, and make a miscalculation or expect a certain cheque to arrive in the mail to cover the amount of the cheque he wrote. He certainly can use arguments of this nature very easily to say that he felt that he had sufficient funds in his account at the time he issued the cheque. It is very difficult for the prosecution or anyone else to contradict an ordinary citizen under these circumstances.
Therefore, an amendment was introduced to what is now subsection 320(4) to cast the burden of proof on the accused that, when issuing the cheque, he had reasonable grounds for believing it would be honoured if presented for payment within a reasonable time.
In simple language, the ordinary citizen has the burden to prove to a court that when he issued the cheque he thought he had the funds in his account. Again, this was to avoid the necessity of providing that at the time the cheque was issued the accused knew that there were insufficient funds on deposit or no funds that would be placed in the account shortly. It was a means for the Crown to establish the guilty knowledge in the mind of the accused which is required for conviction.
The accused may simply rebut this presumption by establishing that at the time he wrote the cheque he had every reason to believe that it would be honoured by his bank. The proposal that is presented by the Member for London East is that a retail establishment, such as a variety store or gas station, would be required under this proposal to give credit, in essence, for a period of at least 15 days from the date upon which the person who wrote the cheque was notified by mail that the cheque was dishonoured. By the time the cheque was deposited in the retailer's account, refused by the bank upon which it is drawn and notification sent to the cheque writer, the total period of grace might be 30 days or more. In practice we know that retailers often provide such a grace period to a person to make good on a bad or n.s.f. cheque before taking action, such as reporting the matter to the police. Most retailers would be happy to extend such a privilege to an ordinary citizen and therefore accomplish the kind of result that the Hon. Member is seeking.
However, there are cases in which prompt action is required to apprehend the truly criminal offender. I agree with the Hon. Member for Edmonton West that an amendment of this nature would open the gates to far more cheque fraud. It would place an impediment in the way of prompt police action to protect other merchants or individuals from being victimized by persons issuing n.s.f. cheques on purpose.

On a point of principle, the effect of this amendment would be inconsistent with the purpose of Section 320. Can we really justify saying to the public that it does not matter whether they knowingly have any funds on account to cover their cheque as long as they made it good within 15 days of being notified by the bank that it was dishonoured?
